oneRepMax.title: 1RM Calculator
oneRepMax.subtitle: Estimate your one-rep max from the weight you lifted and your reps, then get training weights by intensity, plate loading and your big-three total.

safety.title: Train safely
items: Estimates are for reference only. Your real 1RM depends on how you feel, technique and sleep.
Warm up gradually with lighter weights before heavy sets.
Use a spotter or safety bars for bench press and squats.
Stop right away if you feel pain, and talk to a professional first if you have an injury or condition.

u.disclaimer: This calculator is an estimation tool to help plan training and is not medical advice.

formulas.title: The four formulas
items: Epley (1985): 1RM = w × (1 + r/30). From the poundage chart by Nebraska strength coach Boyd Epley, and the most widely used.
Brzycki (1993): 1RM = w × 36/(37 − r). Published by Matt Brzycki in JOPERD. It matches Epley at 10 reps and comes out lower below that.
Lombardi (1989): 1RM = w × r^0.10. Uses a power of the rep count, so it rises slowly with reps and comes out lower at high reps.
O'Conner et al. (1989): 1RM = w × (1 + 0.025r). Adds 2.5% per rep, always below Epley, so it is on the conservative side.
This calculator shows the average of the four as your 1RM, plus each formula's value and the min–max range.

howTo.title: Getting a more accurate estimate
items: Test with a weight you can barely lift 3–10 times. Fewer reps mean a smaller estimation error.
Do one set close to technical failure and enter the weight and the reps you completed.
Warm up well and test on your first heavy set, before fatigue builds up.
A study comparing the bench press, squat and deadlift (LeSuer et al., 1997) found the formulas tended to underestimate the deadlift 1RM.

intensity.title: Choosing training weights by %1RM
items: Strength: 85% of 1RM or more for 6 reps or fewer (NSCA guidance).
Hypertrophy: 67–85% for 6–12 reps.
Muscular endurance: 67% or less for 12+ reps. 50–60% is also common for warm-up sets.
Recalculate your 1RM every few weeks and raise your training weights as it goes up.

bigThree.title: What is the big three total?
items: The sum of your squat, bench press and deadlift 1RMs, the same lifts contested in powerlifting.
People quote totals like "500 kg", but body weight makes a big difference, so a body-weight multiple is a fairer comparison.
Competition lifts are single successful attempts judged to strict standards (squat depth, a pause on the chest in the bench press), so they can differ from estimates.
